newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: United States, Singapore sign open skies accord.
newsitem.headline: United States, Singapore sign open skies accord.

text.p: The United States and Singapore signed an open skies agreement on Tuesday and called on other Asian countries to follow their lead and lift restrictions on air services.

Singapore Communications Minister Mah Bow Tan said the landmark agreement would allow U.S. and Singapore airlines to enjoy unrestricted routing, capacity and frequency between and beyond their borders.

"I hope to see better, more extensive and more competitive air services which will not only benefit customers but also spur the growth of trade, investments and tourism between our two countries," he said.
U.S. Ambassador Timothy Chorba, who signed the pact along with Mah, said Washington hoped the rest of the Asia-Pacific region would follow suit.
"We believe that this agreement will enable airlines to better serve the growing flows of people and cargo between Asia and North America," Chorba said.

"Open aviation accords are the best way to stimulate growth of competitive aviation which best serves our airlines, our customers of aviation services, and the larger economic interests of all nations," he said.

The signature of the pact formalised an agreement initialled in Washington on January 22 and industry analysts said it was likely to increase air services between the two countries and could lower fares.

Singapore is the first Asian country to sign an open skies pact with the United States. Since the agreement was initialled, several other Asian countries have begun talks on the process with the United States.
Seven U.S. carriers operate a combined total of 49 weekly passenger and cargo air services to Singapore.
U.S. airlines flying to Singapore are United Airlines, Northwest Airlines, United Parcel Service, American International Airlines, Polar Air Cargo, Federal Express and Air Micronesia.
Singapore's government-linked carrier, Singapore Airlines (SIA), operates a total of 39 weekly passenger and cargo services to the United States.

The Civil Aviation Authority of Singapore (CAAS) said in a statement annual compound growth rates for air passenger and freight movements between the U.S. and Singapore from 1992 to 1996 were 14.8 percent and 27.4 percent respectively.
Speaking after the ceremony, U.S. Deputy Assistant Secretary for Communications, Mark Gerchick, said open skies agreements allowed markets to set the level of air services and prices.
"To the extent that more carriers serve Singapore one would expect that would have an impact on prices."
Northwest Airlines Southeast Asian regional managing director James Reinnoldt told Reuters the agreement would give airlines extra flexibility in pricing.
"Prices will drop but volumes will increase, so total revenues will increase as well," he said. "That's good for consumers, its good for the airlines and for travel agents."
Analysts said the agreement would increase the pressure on other Asian countries to liberalise their air industries.
"Longer-term, it is positive from SIA's point of view," said Neil Payne, head of research at ING Barings.
SIA's director of corporate affairs, Mathew Samuel, told reporters his company hoped the U.S.-Singapore agreement was the first move towards a multilaterial, regional open skies deal.
"This is a beginning," he said.
